Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

The sunlight was bright, hitting Phainon’s eyes like so many mornings before.

But it was nice, many people had told him the sun suited him.
Maybe in the sense that he needed something… well, someone… who was like a ray of sun hitting him in the eyes.
Some people found it uncomfortable, but the sun had always been something that made people feel awake. Happy, even.

People went out when the sun was shining. People had fun when the sun was shining.
Phainon had always thought of himself as a pluviophile, someone who loves rain, so hearing the words “the sun suits you” was always a bit confusing.
Well, but people also told Mydei that the rain suited him, even though Mydei liked sunny days a lot more.

“Sun and rain make a rainbow anyway,” Phainon grumbled in a tired, almost hushed voice, pulling the blanket a little higher and rolling toward the side where the sun didn’t hit his eyes.
He didn’t want to fall asleep again, really! But his bed was so comfortably warm.
He felt like a cat basking in the sun.

bzz bzz
Just as Phainon was about to close his eyes again, his phone vibrated.
He reached for it on the nightstand, squinting, as the sunlight now hit the bright screen directly, making it harder to see.
Still, he managed to make out the message.

[] Morning, Phai. Thought of you, would you like one?
[] [attached image]

When Phainon tapped on the photo, he was met with… well, a slightly shaky picture.
But he could still make out a cup. From the colors and the ice cubes, it looked like an iced coffee.
It did seem a little low-quality, though — like something bought from a kiosk near some station.

“No way… is he already outside?” Phainon mumbled, finally sitting up and switching back to the chat to type.
But was it really from a kiosk?
He’d never seen Mydei much outside of the café, so he didn’t know his schedule at all.
Some people had early classes, but it was quite rare.

[] Already going to class?

That was the message Phainon finally sent. Not what Mydei was probably hoping for… but Phainon really wanted to know.

[] Yea… The café you work at doesn’t open till later, right?
[] I mean, sometimes it opens early, but whenever I have early classes, it’s closed.
[] Change your damn times, I’m tired of this low-quality coffee!八(•᷄ □•᷅ )

Mydei typed fast—that was the first thing Phainon noticed.
Then there was the kaomoji… those old emoticons hardly anyone used anymore. At least, that’s what Anaxa had told him when he’d once asked about them. Back in the old world, people used them all the time, but seeing someone use them here still caught him off guard.
Phainon started typing, too.

[] It’s not my café. Otherwise, I would change it for you.

“Was that too romantic?” Phainon muttered, staring at the text.
Before he could overthink it, he just hit send.

[] Pfft, quite romantic.

Mydei replied quickly, again, exactly the way Phainon thought he would.
He blushed, looking down, his phone slipping forward to tap against his forehead.

[] I’ll visit after class. Around 11:00 AM.

Right after that message, Phainon checked the time.
8:00 AM.
That meant classes had probably just started for Mydei. Anaxa often texted him that he’d be unavailable from 8:00 to 11:00 because of morning classes, so that must be it.
Another vibration buzzed in his hands.

[] I realllyyyy want a Cinnamon Dolce Latte!

Phainon read it.
Then reread it.
Then… well… again.
“Cinnamon Dolce Latte?” he said out loud, looking up.
They did have that on the menu, but he had never made one before. Ever.
Nobody ordered it, except in the fall and winter seasons, when it was popular.

It wasn’t either of those seasons, so Aglaea had never taught him the basics of the drink.
She’d always said things like “I’ll teach you later” or “It’s too much to handle for you right now.”
She’d also mentioned that, for many baristas — herself included — it was a real pain to make… especially multiple times a day.
Phainon had to memorize so many recipes that he was almost glad she pushed some of them back, but did Mydei have to ask for one now, of all times?

[] In summer?

Phainon replied, trying to gently steer Mydei toward another drink.
He didn’t want to make a fool of himself, especially after making so many drinks that tasted good to Mydei.

[] I know what you’re trying, but I won’t change my mind. Yes, I want it in the summer.

[] Are you making fun of me? You just want to see me fail.

Phainon scoffed as he typed back, maybe a little sassy, but he wanted to confront Mydei playfully.

[] It’s fun. Good luck! (Please make it (シ_ _)シ)

Another kaomoji.
Phainon didn’t reply to this one — partly so Mydei could finally focus on his class, but also because he had to get up for work.
Aglaea still wouldn’t be back, but that didn’t matter.

He had a mission.
And he was ready to do it until it was an SS-tier!

✩₊˚.⋆☾⋆⁺₊✧

The bus ride was lively as always, no, more energetic than usual, to be exact.
People were crammed in shoulder to shoulder, and Phainon didn’t have a chance to sit down at all.
Not that he really needed to… but if one more child plopped into a seat before him, he was this close to pulling them up and taking the seat himself.

Fortunately, his stop was coming up. A few university students stepped off with him, some even greeting him on the way out. He recognized most of their faces—they were regulars at the café.

“Regulars are nice to have...” Phainon muttered, drifting away from the group toward the café.
The Regulars at the café, at least the ones who appreciated the coffee and were kind about it, were nice to have around.
He’d already had to deal with one or two rude customers, cough Castorice cough, but as long as people were nice to each other, it added to the café’s charm.

He unlocked the café door and slipped inside, quickly closing the door again without flipping the “Closed” sign. When the bus stopped nearby, some people seemed to think the place was already open—even when the chairs were still stacked or the pastry display was empty, they stepped inside and just tasked Phainon with any task.
It was frustrating.
So Phainon decided to switch it up and first prepare before flipping the sign at all.

He worked quickly, setting everything in its place, then checked the weather on his phone for once. Rain again today.
“Just a drizzle, but I should be prepared,” he said to himself, absentmindedly fiddling with his hands.

He unfurled the awning and moved the outdoor benches and chairs into a spot safe from the rain, adding cushions. He’d learned some people liked to sit outside even when it rained, and now he was finally prepared for them.
It was Thursday, so he expected more university students than usual.
Once everything was ready, he flipped the sign to “Open” and took his place behind the counter, bracing himself for another long, exhausting day.

First up: making the drink for Mydei.
Step one: Read about it.

Phainon pulled out his phone.
If he was going to make this cinnamon dolce latte, he might as well do it right—Google existed for a reason.

He skimmed through short recipes, picking up tips from baristas on forums. Helpful, at least in theory.
Time to start.

Milk first, because that was the easiest thing to mess up.
Phainon suddenly let out a high-pitched hiss—too sharp, too fast. The jug was colder than he’d realized. Great. Thin foam. Perfect start.
Two shots of espresso followed, a touch more bitter than he liked—fresh beans from the new bag, because he refused to serve old ones. The cinnamon dolce syrup swirled into the cup, darker than it should’ve been, like it had been sitting open just a little too long. Espresso in, milk after—not folding together in a perfect swirl but sloshing into a murky mess.
Cream on top, with a sprinkle of cinnamon to finish. Or at least that was the plan.
The cream came out thin, almost runny, sliding off the foam in a sad collapse. He took one sip, winced, and wrinkled his face as if he’d bitten a lemon.

“That’s what you get for making it yourself,” he muttered.
He set the cup aside.
Round two.

This time, it was going perfectly—milk silky and warm, espresso golden-brown, cinnamon dolce syrup in a flawless spiral. Until the door swung open.
Suddenly, a gust of cold, damp air swept in from the street, and Phainon shivered. His hand jerked mid-pour. The smooth spiral he’d been aiming for broke into a messy splatter, froth pooling unevenly to one side.
Worse, the wind carried the faint smell of wet pavement and bus exhaust, and now he couldn’t shake the idea off that the drink somehow tasted like it, too.
Still technically a cinnamon dolce latte, but the sort you’d expect from a café conveniently located next to a bus stop.

“Fantastic,” he sighed, setting it aside. “At this rate, I’m no better than the other shop Mydei goes to.”
Time passed in a blur of failed attempts. A few university students drifted in, taking shelter from the rain, and the café filled with quiet chatter. Due to so many people coming in, Phainon finally looked at the clock; it was already 10 AM, one hour left until Mydei arrived.
Phainon’s stomach dropped.

“Hey, Phainon?”
He turned.

Cipher, the delivery girl, stood in front of him on the other side of the counter, grinning.
Which was strange—he hadn’t ordered anything.
“I didn’t order a delivery,” he said, trying to sound polite. His face betrayed him, exhaustion written in every line. If the look didn’t give him away, the counter behind him, lined with abandoned cups, definitely did.

Cipher laughed into her hand, pretending not to be too obvious about it. “New décor?” she teased, pointing behind him.

He froze. Oh. Right. Those. He’d forgotten about them completely.
“Ughhh…” The groan that escaped him was loud enough that a couple of students snickered. They’d probably been watching him fail all morning.
“I just want to buy a drink,” Cipher said, still smirking. “Just give me one of those.” She gestured at the cups again.

“Do you think they’re back there for fun? They’re terrible,” he said, genuinely offended at the idea of serving them.
“I don’t care. Give me one. I’ll even take it for free.”

Phainon paused until he finally muttered
“At least it’ll be gone,” handing one over.
Cipher accepted it, then hesitated. “Uh… I need it to go.”
He poured it half-heartedly into a paper cup. “Here.”
She took a sip.

A Pause.
A longer Pause.
Too much of a long pause.
Then she looked up at him.

“…I want to throw up,” she finally said.

“UGHHHHH.” Phainon almost yanked off his apron. He buried his face in his hands, willing himself not to scream.
Cipher, unfazed, took another sip. “Just call Aglaea.”
“That would be the first time I’ve ever done that,” he muttered, unlocking his phone.
She gave him a thumbs up and strolled out to her delivery van, leaving him with a counter full of failures and less than an hour until Mydei walked through the door.

If he didn’t call, he’d fail. If he did call, maybe—just maybe—he’d make the best cinnamon dolce latte Mydei had ever tasted.
Phainon let himself imagine how Mydei praised him for a moment, right before heading into the back room to make the call.

✩₊˚.⋆☾⋆⁺₊✧

One ring.
Two rings.
By the third ring, Phainon was already impatient.
Finally, Aglaea picked up.

Phainon instantly tripped over his words, stumbling into a mess of gibberish.
“You sound desperate,” she said—clipped, efficient, the kind of voice that already had a hundred solutions lined up.
“I am desperate!” Phainon blurted. “I’ve been making swamp water all morning. One guy is coming in less than an hour, and if I serve him this—” he gestured wildly at the cups, though she couldn’t see them, “—he’ll never come back!”

Aglaea raised a brow on her end, surprised at how much he sounded like someone panicking before a date, but she recovered quickly.
“Breathe.” Her voice softened, just barely. “What are you trying to make?”
“Cinnamon dolce latte.”
“In summer?” she asked, skeptical.
Phainon nodded, even though she couldn’t see it.

“And it looks like… swamp water?” she added, holding back a giggle.
“Yes! And it tastes like it too!”
“Did you check if the steam wand you insisted on fixing yourself instead of calling me last week is the problem?”
Phainon froze, mortified. “…Maybe.”

“Gods, Phai.” Aglaea groaned. “When’s this so-called guy getting here?”
“In a few minutes. I only have one chance…” he muttered.
She let out a long, theatrical groan.
“Okay. Go to the counter. We’ll fix this together. Just do exactly as I say.”
Relief hit him like a wave. “You’re a lifesaver.”
“No,” she corrected flatly. “I’m the reason you’ll still have a chance with him by lunch.”

Phainon hurried out front and grabbed a cup, phone pressed to his ear.
“Okay, I’ve got the espresso—”
“Stop. Did you taste it?”
“…No?”
“Then taste it. If the base is bad, everything after is wasted.”
He took a sip, grimaced, then admitted, “It’s good.”

“Good. Sweetness hides bitterness, not disaster. Now grab the cinnamon syrup. Not the cheap stuff—the one I gave you.”
Phainon almost facepalmed. Right. She’d given him extra bottles for fancy orders. He fumbled around until he found it. “I got the one.”

“Two tablespoons. Stir it into the espresso until it looks like melted bronze. Don’t just swirl—stir.”
He stirred furiously, splashing a little on the counter, but it wasn't enough to call it a waste. “Done.”
“Now steam the milk. And I swear, Phai, if you burn it—”
“I won’t!” he shot back, nearly burning it.

“Tip the jug just enough to get a whirlpool. You want microfoam, not soap bubbles. Think silk, not dishwater.”
He steadied himself, breath tight, until finally the milk smoothed into a glossy swirl.
“Now pour slowly. First, the milk, then ease the foam on top. Control it. Don’t dump it like soup.”
Phainon tsked as if he didn't already know that, though his tongue stuck out in concentration as he poured.

The result… actually looked decent.
“…It actually looks good?” he said, almost in disbelief.
Aglaea chuckled on the other end. “It should. Now finish it—whipped cream, drizzle of syrup, dusting of cinnamon. Make it look like it belongs in a window display.”
He followed her instructions, stepping back at last. Under the café lights, the drink gleamed, crowned with cream and spice.

“…That’s… beautiful.”
“Of course it is. You followed directions for once. Now don’t ruin it before your guy gets there.”
There was a pause, long enough that Phainon thought she’d hung up.
“Oh, and when I’m back,” she added casually, “you’re telling me all about him.” Then she ended the call.

Phainon smiled—until he glanced at the clock. His eyes widened. With a frantic shuffle, he began hiding every failed attempt, leaving only the perfect latte on the counter like it had always been the only one.

Just as he shoved the last swamp-water cup into the sink, the bell above the door chimed.
Phainon straightened so fast he nearly knocked over the one perfect drink. His heart leapt into his throat.

And there he was.
The guy.
His Mydei.

"Up and ready to serve, sir," Phainon said, as if he were a butler serving his master. Shoving the Drink a bit more to the front so Mydei can see that it's ready.

Mydei raised a brow, the corner of his mouth twitching like he was suppressing a laugh. “Since when do you call me sir?”
Phainon froze, realizing how absurd he sounded. “Uh—I mean—customer service?” His voice cracked halfway through the excuse.

Mydei stepped closer to the counter, eyes catching on the latte like a hawk spotting prey. He leaned down, inhaling the cinnamon and sweet cream, then let out a low whistle. “This… looks impressive. Did you finally sell your soul to the coffee gods?”
Phainon forced a laugh that came out more like a squeak. “Something like that.” He slid the cup forward with as much poise as he could fake. “Cinnamon dolce latte. House special, just like you wanted!"

Mydei’s hand wrapped around the cup, fingers brushing the cardboard sleeve—and for a brief, electric second, brushing Phainon’s too.
The warmth lingered longer than the touch itself, and Phainon nearly forgot how to breathe.
Mydei took a slow sip. His expression was unreadable at first—then, his eyes widened.

“…Phai.” He said his name as if it were a revelation. “This is really good.”
Relief thundered through Phainon so hard he had to grip the counter to keep his knees from buckling. “Y-you think so?”

“Think so? No. I know so.” Mydei lifted the cup slightly, like a toast. “Best thing I’ve had all summer. Hands down.”
Phainon flushed so red he was glad the café lights weren’t too harsh. “Well, I… uh… aim to please.”
Mydei chuckled, and for a heartbeat, his gaze softened in a way that made the whole disastrous morning worth it.

Then, casually, like it was no big deal, he added, “Guess I’ll have to come back again soon, huh?”
Phainon’s heart skipped. He grinned, trying not to look too triumphant, but then Phainon noticed what Mydei exactly said and looked at him in panic. “Wait, are you leaving already?!"

Phainon’s eyes widened, bright and expectant, like a puppy that had been waiting all day. Mydei stared back, his lips pulling into a downward smile—as if he wanted to act tough, but couldn’t quite manage it.

“Well, I still have stuff to do at home… I didn’t plan this at all. I wanted to stay, but…” Mydei rubbed the back of his neck, sheepish and nervous, “It’s better if I get it done today since I’ve got a free day tomorrow.”
It felt wrong to leave already.
Mydei really did enjoy spending time with Phainon, but maybe both of them were afraid—afraid that a few hours apart might cool the spark, or worse, that the other might lose interest.
Phainon blinked, catching up to what Mydei had just said.

“Wait—you have a free day tomorrow?” His surprise was obvious. Those were rare words from Mydei.
“Yeah. Every Friday, actually. I know, odd.” Mydei took another sip of the latte, almost casually.
“That… sucks,” Phainon mumbled, the last word barely audible.
Silence hovered for a moment.
Then Mydei tilted his head, eyes warm and steady. “Do you work late tomorrow?”

Phainon met his gaze and shook his head quickly. “Not really. We actually close earlier than usual.”
That earned him a slow, growing smile from Mydei—like he’d just stumbled onto a brilliant idea.
“Then… come over to my place.”

BOOM.
Phainon’s heart—or maybe his entire brain—exploded.
His what?
He should go to where?
From who?

“I should… come… what? To where? From who? From You?” Phainon stumbled over his words again. This was becoming a far too regular occurrence.
“My place. Tomorrow… if you’re up for it, at least.”

Phainon almost jumped over the counter—well, he sort of did. He leaned in close, close enough that their faces were inches apart, their breaths mingling.
“You smell like warm sand,” Mydei murmured, eyes scanning him from head to toe.
“And you… like pomegranate,” Phainon replied with a shy smile, adding his own teasing twist.
By now, everyone in the café could probably tell something was happening.

Phainon pulled back slightly, not wanting to crowd Mydei, though he noticed, too late, that Mydei looked a touch disappointed.
“I can come! I’ll just work, close up, and then I can come straight to you,” Phainon said, practically glowing. Mydei nodded and reached out, ruffling Phainon’s hair. Soft. So soft.

“Sure. Please text me a specific time, though. I don’t want to be unprepared.” And just like that, Mydei left the café, without a proper goodbye, leaving Phainon standing there, heart racing.

Prepare? Prepare for what?
“I… I can prepare you,” Phainon muttered under his breath, a blush creeping across his cheeks as he imagined what that could mean.

Since it was now 11:30, Phainon continued his routine: cleaning after customers, helping them, setting up some music in the café. His usual routine, you might say.

But in Phainon’s head, there was chaos—so much chaos that it was unbearable to work any longer. He wanted to run home, shower, and even wear a suit to go see Mydei.
Would that be too much?
God, he needed some advice…
He thought about it.

Anaxa? No way—he would help, but he’s so… boomer-like.
Aglaea? No, asking for advice again would only make her want more and more details.
Castorice? NO! She would laugh more than help.
Cipher? Well… she’s mostly a bystander and wouldn’t know anything.
Hm…

He stared at his work phone a few times, googling: “What should you do when your crush invites you to their home?”
The answers were either:
"Don’t trust them!! Why invite you to their house first?"
or
"Getting you alone in their home at night is no way to get to know someone as a gentleman."
God, he wasn’t even a girl—why are people so serious? Well, they did have a point… at least if Phainon were a girl.

So his next question was: “What should you wear on your first date?”
That helped a lot more this time.
"Something comfortable and that fits the mood." Well, if it was in the house, then something comfy would be good, huh?
But he still had open questions.

Should he bring gifts?
When is he supposed to leave? IS HE EVEN SUPPOSED TO LEAVE?
Should he suggest what they do, or will Mydei?
Is staying at home a way of saying they’ll just stay in the neighborhood, or literally just stay at home?

Both would be fine. Mydei should rest, but… UGH.
As the day slowly went by, it was already closing time, which meant the usual: cleaning EVERYTHING! Tables, chairs, moving everything from outside to inside.

But this time, with a twist: he had his phone to his ear again. He dialed the number of the oh-so-mysterious "Pastry Girl (DO NOT TRUST, MAKE IT YOURSELF!)" aka Cipher.
She picked up fast. She was always bored at work—you could notice it instantly when talking to her.
Having someone on speaker while she worked was fun for her. Well, for Phainon too, of course, even though he wished it were Mydei on the other side.

"So, what do you need?" she finally asked. They had been on the phone for around thirty minutes, but Cipher had just yapped about customers and what she would do when she finally got home. Stuff that Phainon never asked for.

"Yeah, I have a… sort of date? Tomorrow," he said, a bit confused, not even knowing how to call it.
Cipher laughed out loud. "Wow, is your imagination running high? I bet they didn’t mean it like that," she said, giggling.
"Ha ha, funny," he said and grabbed the broom from storage, so there was a small pause. "I just need advice," he continued.

"Advice?" Cipher echoed, her tone half-amused, half-curious. "For what exactly? Because from the way you’re talking, it sounds like a full-on panic situation."

Phainon groaned, rubbing the back of his neck. "Yeah… I mean, it’s not really… I don’t even know. He invited me over. To his place. And I don’t know what to do, what to wear, if I should bring anything… I don’t even know how long I’m supposed to stay. It’s—" He waved the broom vaguely, even though Cipher couldn’t see it. "It’s chaos."

Cipher’s laugh came again, this time softer, like she was trying not to sound too harsh. "Oh, Coffee Boy. You make it sound like you’re going to a dragon’s lair instead of a friend’s house."
"Does it sound that bad?" he muttered, a bit wounded.
"Yes… and no," she said, sighing theatrically. "Listen, just take a deep breath. It’s just… a guy. Not the king of some intergalactic empire. You don’t need armor or a strategy for war."

Phainon hesitated, broom frozen mid-swipe. "Well, for me, he is a king."
Quite literally, at least in the other world.
"Doesn’t matter," Cipher said, practically rolling her eyes. "Just wear comfortable clothes, maybe something you’d actually feel good in if you had to sit on the floor or eat snacks off the counter. Don’t overthink gifts—if you want, maybe something small and thoughtful. Nothing that screams, ‘I Googled this for three hours.’"

Phainon scribbled mental notes, but another worry bubbled up. "What about… what we do? Do I… suggest things?"
Cipher chuckled, this time with a hint of mischief. "If he invited you, he probably has an idea. But you can throw out suggestions if you want. Like, ‘Hey, want to watch that show we talked about?’ or ‘I can help you make that crazy recipe you mentioned.’ Keep it casual. No need for full-on event planning."

Phainon exhaled. It didn’t feel like chaos anymore—just nervous anticipation. "And… leaving? How do I… I don’t want to overstay."
"Simple," Cipher said, as if stating an undeniable fact. "When it feels like a good time to leave, leave. If he says ‘stay longer,’ awesome. If not, that’s fine too. You’re not trapped in some polite hostage situation."
Phainon chuckled, a little awkwardly, but there was a lightness now. "…I think I can handle that."

"Of course you can," Cipher said, more softly now, almost like she was letting him in on a secret. "Just… don’t overthink it. It’s not a test. It’s… you, and him, just hanging out."
Phainon leaned on the broom, a tiny smile creeping onto his face. For the first time that day, the chaos in his head seemed… manageable. Almost exciting, even.

"Thanks… Cipher," he muttered. "Really. I mean, even if you laugh at me."
She snorted. "Hey, laughing at you is my cardio. But seriously… you’ve got this. Now, finish cleaning. Don’t let the gods see you panic too much."
He chuckled, thanking her.
"Tell me if I can repay you somehow," he said.
She slowly exhaled and thought. "I know the last guy gave me a weird name on the phone, please change it. It’s weird when Aglaea sees it because she might think I’m unreliable." She sounded almost like she was begging.

Phainon instantly renamed her on the phone: "Cipher’s Pastries (quite nice.)"
He told her it was done, and they hung up.

As Phainon flipped the "Open" sign to "Closed," he almost skipped all the way home, feeling so happy about what had happened, even though the day had felt long without Mydei around. Tomorrow, they would have a long day together!

That is, until he remembered… HE HAD TO TELL MYDEI THE TIME HE WOULD COME TOMORROW!
Phainon quickly grabbed his phone and texted Mydei:

[]Hey, I will come to you at around 12 PM tomorrow, okay? If it’s too early, please tell me…｡ﾟ(TヮT)

And finally, he sent it.
As he boarded the bus, Mydei texted back quickly:

[]Hi Phai, no worries! I wake up pretty early on Fridays, so the time should be fine—it’s noon after all! Here’s my address: █████

[]Thank u! I’m very excited for tomorrow.

With that, he enjoyed the rest of the bus ride, just checking how long it would take him to get there on time.
As Phainon arrived home, he didn’t immediately shower, eat, and fall into bed.
No! He had to prepare. He grabbed a backpack and packed some extra clothes, so he wouldn’t go to Mydei in his dirty work clothes.
He also put in some perfume to apply after work, mentally noting to shower again in the morning to smell good.

✩₊˚.⋆☾⋆⁺₊✧

The next morning, Phainon woke up with the sun streaming through his window. His alarm hadn’t even gone off yet—he’d already been awake for half an hour, just staring at the ceiling and thinking about Mydei.

His mind kept circling back to the same questions: “Did I say the right thing in the message? Is 12 too early? What if I mess things up?”
He shook his head, trying to clear the spiraling thoughts. Today wasn’t a day for chaos—at least, not the same kind of chaos as yesterday. Today was… manageable chaos.

After a quick shower, he slipped into his work clothes and grabbed something to eat. He definitely didn’t want to go to Mydei’s place in a hungry state. Breakfast was rushed, just coffee and toast, but even then, his thoughts wandered constantly to the visit ahead.
“What if he doesn’t like the snacks I bring? Maybe it’s better to bring flowers… but what if he’s allergic in this universe?”

Phainon grumbled at his own overthinking. He knew he wouldn’t stop worrying until he actually arrived.
Still, he spritzed on some perfume—already knowing he’d need to reapply it later anyway—and stepped out of the house.
Practically running to the bus stop, he felt a buzz of energy in his chest. Today he only had to work for four hours, which meant he wouldn’t be too tired by the time he got to Mydei. The thought gave him a boost of motivation.

Catching the bus, Phainon made it to the café and opened up as quickly as possible. He moved faster than usual, taking orders, making drinks, and clearing tables with a kind of nervous efficiency. So much so that a few customers actually asked if something special was going on.

Phainon wanted to explode and tell them everything, but… that would be weird, wouldn’t it? So he just nodded and said, “We’re closing early today. I want to at least get some orders done first.” Then he turned right back to work—more orders, more drinks, more cleaning.

The hours ticked by faster than he expected.
Before long, the café was winding down, and the “Closed” sign was flipped with a satisfying clack.
Phainon leaned against the counter for a moment, heart thudding.

That’s it.
No more distractions.
Next stop: Mydei.

He slipped off his apron, grabbed his backpack from the back room, and checked it for the tenth time—extra clothes, notebook, perfume. Everything was in place.

Pulling out the fresh clothes, he ducked into the café’s bathroom to change.
A crisp white shirt, light blue pants, and a simple brown belt to finish the touch.
He stepped back out, tugging at the fabric and checking his reflection in the Mirror. He had only packed them quickly, half-afraid they wouldn’t fit. To his relief, they actually looked good.

Back at his bag, he grabbed the perfume, re-applied it, and gave his hair a half-hearted attempt at flattening in the reflection of the coffee machine. With a deep breath, Phainon finally locked the café door behind him.
This time, he walked the opposite way.

Usually, he watched Mydei head down this road. Does that sound stalkery? he asked himself, grimacing.
Shaking the thought off, he opened the map app, typed in Mydei’s address, and followed the path to the train station.
Ticket bought. Platform found. Everything seemed to go smoothly… until the announcements began.

"The train has problems, so it needs more time."
"Sorry, we have an overhead line issue."
"The train is delayed due to… a curse we can’t figure out."

“Oh, fucking sure,” Phainon muttered under his breath. He paced around the station, fighting the urge to text Mydei and confess how badly this was going already.
But then—finally—the train arrived. Relief rushed through him so strongly it almost made him laugh. He boarded quickly and sank into a seat, staring at the screen that showed the upcoming stops. So far, so good.
At least, that’s what he thought.

A group of children started running around the carriage, shrieking and laughing. One tiny child, cradled in their mother’s arms, carried a bottle of milk—until, of course, it slipped from their hands and spilled right onto Phainon.
Just his luck.

“I’m so sorry, young man!” the mother gasped, setting the child down and fumbling with tissues to dab at his shirt.
Phainon forced a polite smile, waving his hands. “Ma’am, it’s okay, really. It happens. Kids don’t have much strength when they’re distracted.”
He glanced down at his shirt—stained, damp—but quickly looked away again, pretending he still looked perfectly fine. Maybe if he believed it hard enough, others would too.

Once the mother calmed down, he checked the screen again… only to feel his stomach drop.
His stop wasn’t there anymore.
He had missed it.
“Ugh!!” Phainon groaned, slumping back in his seat.

A glance at the clock told him he still had some time. Enough to change trains, at least.
At the next station, he hopped off, hurried to the opposite platform, and caught the next train going back. Thankfully, it pulled in right away. Within minutes, he was finally—finally—back at the correct stop.
Note to himself: never trust trains again.

Inside the station were a few shops. He dashed into one, buying flowers, and into another for snacks. With his spoils stuffed into his bag, he stepped outside…
…just in time for the sky to open up.

Drop.
Drop.
Drop drop.

Rain splattered against his face, one drop landing directly in his eye.
“Are you kidding me?” Phainon groaned, resisting the urge to scream into the downpour. He had no jacket, no umbrella. Clutching his backpack in his arms like a shield, he tucked the flowers and snacks inside to keep them safe.

His phone, map still glowing, was quickly shoved into his pocket before the rain could ruin it.
From what he remembered, the map had shown a straight path. Just down the road, first apartment building. Mydei’s place.
So Phainon ran.

He sprinted through the rain, shoes slapping against the pavement, hair plastered to his forehead. He had once sworn running in the rain was pointless—it only made you wetter.
But right now? He didn’t care.
At least, he thought with a bitter little laugh, he no longer smelled like milk.
And if he showed up late, at least he’d have an excuse.

Chapter End Notes

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Phainon tore down the street, lungs on fire, shoes squelching like sponges with every miserable step. Houses blurred past in a watercolor smear until
Finally.
There it finally was.

He slowed, squinting through his eyelashes that were heavy with rain, and blinked at the tree swaying outside the gate. A pomegranate tree.

"Of course he owns a hou-"
Suddenly, water shot straight up his nose.
“—hhhk!” Phainon hacked, coughing so hard that he nearly doubled over. His hands slapped at his face, water streaming everywhere. When he finally forced his eyes open, the numbers on the gate gleamed through the downpour.
Yep. Mydei’s house.

Bent over, palms on knees, he tried to steady the ragged wheeze of his breath. His once-crisp shirt was now glued to his body, his hair dripping into his eyes like sad wet noodles. Hopefully the flowers survived—somehow at least, despite the storm.

“Well, I hope at least something looks good...” he muttered. Half-smile. Half-misery. He reached for the bell—
Footsteps. Sharp, fast, splashing through the puddles.
Phainon jerked his head up.
And there he was.

Mydei. An umbrella cutting a circle of dryness above him, black pants, short-sleeved shirt… and Crocs.
Mydeis' expression was carved out of worry and sheer panic.
“PHAINON, ARE YOU OKAY?” he shouted.

Phainon cracked. Laughter bubbled out of him, wild and breathless, shaking his drenched shoulders. He must have looked like a drowned rat dragged from the riverbank.
“I—I-I’m fine,” he gasped, bent double with giggles. “Just… soggy.”
Mydei blinked. Then his chest deflated with a sharp exhale, a reluctant smile tugging at his mouth. “You’re insane. Come on—get in.”

The umbrella didn’t help much now, but when Mydei opened the gate and tilted it toward him, warmth hit Phainon’s chest harder than the rain ever had.

Inside, as he peeled off his squelching shoes, Phainon blinked.
There was a genkan.
It was a proper entryway, neat and deliberate, like the kind he’d only ever seen in Japanese houses online. A little space just for pausing, shoes off, world left at the door.
“...Huh,” he murmured, lips quirking despite the rain dripping down his neck. “That’s… actually pretty cool.”
It fit Mydei—structured, thoughtful, subtle. A place that made sense.
Phainon almost laughed.
Of course, Mydei’s house would have rules, even in the floor plan.

Then, right after he got his shoes and backpack off, he heard soft pawsteps that padded over the wooden floor. He glanced up. On the stairs, an orange cat surveyed him like royalty. Regal. Judgmental.
Right. Mydei had a lion once. Mimi. So—

“Ah, just ignore Mimi,” Mydei said casually, shaking the rain from the umbrella.
Phainon’s grin slipped out. “So it really is Mimi, huh…” He couldn’t stop chuckling.
A lion in one world, a queen in the next. Perfect.

Before he could linger, Mydei tugged him down the hall. Cozy wooden floors, shelves bursting with books, a fireplace whispering in the corner—and then, suddenly, a towel smacked onto his head.
“Dry off before you ruin my floors,” Mydei said.
Phainon snorted into the terrycloth. “Sorry. Didn’t plan for a storm ambush.”
“Ambush?” Mydei arched a brow from the sink. “The clouds declared war on you?”
“Feels like it.” He scrubbed at his hair, cheeks glowing pink in the mirror.

His shirt clung pitifully, but his grin refused to fade.
When he lowered the towel, Mydei was rummaging in the cabinet. Out came folded clothes—grey sweatpants, a navy blue shirt, and a fitting pair of socks.
“Here. Not your style, but you won’t catch a cold.”
Phainon’s heart stuttered like a faulty engine. “You’re… lending me your clothes?”
“Would you rather freeze?”
“…No.”
“Thought so.” Mydei shoved the bundle into his arms and nodded to the door. “Change. I’ll make tea.”

The bathroom door shut. Phainon pressed the clothes to his chest, heat crawling up his neck. He laughed under his breath.
He was in Mydei’s house.
About to wear Mydei’s clothes.
Impossible. Stupid. Perfect.

“Meow.”
Phainon jumped. Mimi was perched in the sink now, glaring like a monarch surveying her newest fool.
“Too scary, Mimi,” he whispered, slipping into the clothes. He scooped her up, her tail flicking with imperious grace. “Do you remember me, hmm?”
No answer, just a blank stare.

✩₊˚.⋆☾⋆⁺₊✧

As Phainon padded into the kitchen, he slowed. Mydei was still at the counter, movements precise, steam curling around him. Not the usual dunk-a-bag-in-hot-water routine either—this looked… deliberate. Loose leaf, measured by hand, stirred with care.
Phainon wasn't surprised. Mydei never did anything halfway.

Without turning, Mydei said, “If you want, you could… explore the house.”
Phainon blinked. His chest gave one of those traitorous stutters.
Explore the house? That sounded way too private. Like opening a diary without asking.
But—if Mydei was offering, if Mydei trusted him like that—there was no way he could refuse.

“…Anything off-limits?” he asked carefully.
A short scoff, Mydei’s shoulders rising once. He shook his head.
Phainon swallowed, cheeks heating up once again as he turned away. “Alright then,” he muttered, heart rattling like he was about to commit a crime instead of… wander a hallway.
He went. On tiptoe, like the house itself was listening.

He immediately noticed attributes,
back in the living room, details leapt out: beams polished warm brown, books stacked in chaotic order, spaces open where doors might once have been. Not a palace. Not a throne. Just a home. A place built for life.
How silly. How right.

The arched doorframe that opened from the kitchen into the living room was wide, almost extravagant, like it had been built with the idea that a whole family should pour through it together.

Just beside it, a narrower frame led back toward the hallway—more practical, more reserved.
The living room itself breathed warmth. A sofa in a muted orange sat beneath the soft glow of the lamps, scattered with mismatched pillows and a blue-and-white blanket that looked well-loved.

A matching armchair was drawn up close, angled in such a way that Phainon could imagine Mydei reading there on rainy evenings. Between them, a fluffy carpet stretched across the floor, anchoring a low wooden table scarred with the kind of marks that came from actual use.

Against the far wall, a fireplace flickered gently, the hearth neat and clean. Above it, mounted just high enough to avoid the heat, hung a TV—modern convenience layered over old comfort. To his left, a window bench rested beneath the tall panes, books stacked haphazardly on its surface.

A few leafy plants leaned toward the drizzle outside, taking advantage of the window cracked just enough to let the rain-scented air in. Not enough to soak anything—just enough to feed green life.
Phainon’s eyes wandered back to the arch, and there he saw the dining nook tucked neatly at the edge of the living room. Modest, functional, with only a few chairs. Not the kind of place meant for crowds. This was a house built for one, maybe two.

The food bowls on the floor caught his attention—raised smartly, clearly placed with Mimi in mind.
On the opposite wall hung photographs: Mydei in different snapshots of time, surrounded by groups of friends, laughter frozen mid-burst, arms slung over shoulders. A collage of lives lived together.
Phainon’s chest tightened, his arms shifting slightly as Mimi purred against him. “I wish I could’ve been here earlier…” he murmured, almost afraid the house itself might overhear. His shoulders slumped as the words left him, honest in a way he hadn’t meant them to be.
A few cabinets lined the walls as well—closed, orderly. He didn’t dare open them. That felt too much like trespassing.

And besides, he still held Mimi, her weight warm and grounding in his arms. She blinked at him with her slow, imperious calm, as though she, too, was part of the house he was learning.

“Phai—”
He looked up. Mydei froze mid-step, two mugs in hand. His brow creased.
“What? Do I look that bad?” Phainon asked, half a laugh already in his throat.
“No. Just… Mimi never lets strangers hold her.” Mydei’s voice was low, almost careful. “Usually she runs away.”
Phainon’s chest went molten. He swallowed the brag that wanted to spill and said softly, “Then I’m honored.”
That earned him a smile.

“Or maybe you talked about me so much she already knows me.” The tease slipped out before Phainon could stop it.
Mydei froze. His ears flushed red. And then—he turned tail, retreating to the kitchen as if escape was the only option.
Phainon grinned, teeth flashing.
Score!

✩₊˚.⋆☾⋆⁺₊✧

As he celebrated his victory, he remembered the flowers in his bag.
He let Mimi go as he quickly went to the front door and fished them out, brushing petals back into place, hesitating at the archway. Was it stupid to give them now? Too much? Too soon?
The smell of herbs—rosemary, thyme—drifted from the kitchen. Warmth threaded the air. Phainon took a breath and stepped through.
“Uh,” he began, voice cracking. He lifted the flowers like a shield. “These are… for you. I didn’t want to come empty-handed.”

Mydei froze again. His gaze caught on the blooms, expression unreadable. Then—soft. Too soft.
“…You carried those through the rain?”
Phainon’s grin tilted crooked. “They survived better than me.”
Something twitched at Mydei’s mouth, like a smile breaking against his will. He crossed the distance, fingers brushing the petals. “…You’re ridiculous.”
“And yet you’re smiling.”

Color bloomed on Mydei’s cheeks. He took the bouquet carefully, as if it existed in a fragile state. “…I’ll find a vase.”
Mimi leapt onto the counter, sniffed, and dismissed.
“Guess Mimi disapproves,” Phainon said.
“She thinks she owns everything,” Mydei muttered, tucking the flowers into a glass vase with practiced ease.
“You get flowers often?”
A sharp glance. A scoff. “Hardly. Not like this.”
Not like this. The words stuck. Heavy.

Phainon leaned into the archway, warmth settling deep in his ribs. Storm outside, gentleness inside.
“So… what’ll we do?” he asked, trying to be casual.

“I’ve got some games. Or a movie. I would’ve taken you to the café nearby but…” Mydei gestured at the window. The rain lashed harder, blurring the glass.
“Guess it’s just us three,” Phainon said, scooping Mimi back up.
And Mydei’s smile—it was so bright, like the storm hadn’t touched him.

“…Games, then a movie?” Phainon offered, brain buzzing. Don’t overthink. Don’t stay too long. Don’t ruin this.
Too late—his skull was already buzzing with questions. Was this too much? Not enough? Was he supposed to leave soon?

This was chaos.
But at least it was the good kind.
At least—it was a date, he hoped.

“Sounds good. Very romantic,” Mydei murmured as he stepped into the living room, steam still curling from his mug. He set it down with care, then all but collapsed into the couch like it had been waiting for him all day.

Phainon followed, lips twitching. “What—pretending you cleaned the whole house?” he teased, a low chuckle slipping out.
It lasted only for three seconds, though.
Because Mydei’s head turned. A look. A glare so sharp it sliced straight through Phainon’s laugh.

“…Wait. Did you—?” Phainon froze, eyes wide.
Mydei only leaned back into the cushions, arms folding, the tiniest spark of smugness glinting in his expression. He nodded once. Slow.
Oh no. He actually had.

Phainon’s mouth opened, closed. Heat rushed up his face.
Meanwhile, Mydei sat there, proud as a cat with a caught bird—but just the faintest pout tugged at his lips, like he’d expected more. Praise. Awe. At least one gasp of wow, you did all this for me?

Phainon swallowed. “...I. Uh. Okay. That’s… impressive,” he managed, voice cracking just enough to make Mydei’s brow twitch.

Phainon rubbed the back of his neck, staring at Mydei like he’d just confessed to running a marathon for fun. “I mean—don’t get me wrong, it looks great. Spotless. Cozy. Like, uh…”
He gestured vaguely at the gleaming table, the fluffed pillows, the lack of dust anywhere. “…like someone lives here who isn’t a total disaster.”
Mydei’s pout deepened. “That’s your idea of a compliment?”

Phainon winced. “Okay, okay, wait—restart. Let me try again.” He shifted on the couch, sitting straighter, clearing his throat as if announcing something very official. “Mydei, this house is beautiful. But what’s really beautiful is the fact that you, in all your wisdom, prepared for my soggy, chaotic arrival by scrubbing every corner of it like an overachieving saint.”

Finally, there it was. The flicker of a smile, quick and reluctant, tugging at the corners of Mydei’s mouth.
“You’re ridiculous,” Mydei muttered, reaching for his mug. But his ears were pink, and he wouldn’t look directly at Phainon.
Which made it all the easier for Phainon to lean in, grinning wide now. “And yet, you’re smiling.”

That earned him a low groan. Mydei tugged the blanket off the back of the couch and threw it over Phainon’s head, burying him in blue fluff. “Shut up and drink your tea.”
Phainon’s muffled laugh came through the fabric. He peeked out, hair sticking up at odd angles, eyes shining. “Only if you promise not to glare at me anymore.”
“I make no promises,” Mydei said, but the warmth in his voice betrayed him.

Not even if I asked you… If we could be together forever?”
The words slipped out of Phainon’s mouth like steam from his tea—casual, unthinking. By the time the sentence hung in the air, he was already sipping as if nothing had happened.

Mydei, however, nearly died on the spot. He choked, coughed, and almost spilled his mug, eyes wide in shock.
Phainon shot up straighter. “What’s wrong?!” He leaned in, panicked, ready to perform first aid if necessary.
Mydei finally managed to breathe again, wiping his mouth with the back of his hand. His gaze cut to Phainon, sharp and searching. “What… did you just say?”
Phainon blinked. “Uh—what’s wrong?”
Silence.

Mydei dragged a hand down his face, muttering something halfway between a curse and a groan. He had heard perfectly. The idiot just didn’t realize what he’d said.
Still flushed red, Mydei shifted, eyes darting anywhere but Phainon. “…Yes. And… maybe I could keep some promises.” The words were soft, begrudging, but honest.

Phainon tilted his head, still blank, still clueless.
“Wait, what?”
Mydei let his head thunk back against the couch, covering his face entirely.

How was he supposed to fall for someone who couldn’t even remember confessing?

Phainon blinked at him, Mimi purring in his lap like nothing world-shaking had just happened. “You okay? You’re acting weird.”

Mydei groaned louder, dragging the blanket over his own head this time. “Unbelievable.”
“What is?” Phainon leaned closer, tugging at the blanket, but Mydei only held it tighter around his face. His ears were glowing red through the fabric.

“You don’t even hear yourself,” came the muffled reply.
Phainon frowned. “Hear me say what?”
Another groan, this one almost theatrical. Mydei threw the blanket off again, sitting upright and jabbing a finger at him. “You just dropped a forever bomb like it was small talk! And then you forgot!”
Phainon froze, tea halfway to his mouth. “...I did?”
“Yes!”
“Oh.” He blinked once. Twice. Then, to Mydei’s horror, he smiled. A slow, shy little smile that lit his whole face. “Well… I guess that means I meant it.”

Mydei’s heart lurched so hard he thought the blanket might actually combust from the heat in his chest. He opened his mouth—closed it again—looked away before Phainon could see how rattled he really was.
“…Idiot,” he muttered, softer this time.
Phainon grinned wider, sinking into the couch beside him until their shoulders brushed. “Yeah. But I’m your idiot.”
Mydei nearly dropped the mug all over again.

“So what game do you want to play?” Mydei asked, flicking through the menu as the Switch came to life.
“I don’t know, hit me with it,” Phainon said, settling deeper into the couch, mug in one hand, Mimi curled up in the other like a fuzzy armrest.
Mydei scrolled, eyes narrowing thoughtfully. “Alright. But no whining when I destroy you.”

Phainon arched a brow. “Destroy me? Please. You’re forgetting—I grew up with this stuff. I’m basically a gaming prodigy.”
“That so?” Mydei clicked into a racing game, the sound effects filling the room. “Then this should be easy for you.”
The controllers synced. The screen lit up. The countdown started.
Three. Two. One.

They shot off the starting line, colors blurring across the TV.
“Hey—that’s cheating!” Phainon yelped as Mydei’s character rammed him off the track within seconds.
“Cheating? It’s called skill,” Mydei said smoothly, leaning back with maddening calm while his racer zipped ahead.
Phainon leaned forward, eyes narrowing, tongue caught between his teeth as he tried to recover. “You’re gonna regret that. I’m the comeback king.”

“Mmhm. Keep telling yourself that.”
When Phainon’s car exploded in a fiery spinout a moment later, he threw his hands up dramatically, nearly spilling his tea. “WHAT is with this game?!”
Mydei laughed—an actual laugh, unguarded and bright—and it hit Phainon harder than any in-game crash. He found himself grinning like an idiot even as he lost again.

“Best two out of three,” Phainon declared.
“Already making excuses?” Mydei teased, passing him another controller.
Phainon smirked. “No. Just giving you a head start before I destroy you.”
"Oh, where I wonder~ not in this game at least!" Mydei giggled, and Phainon blushed, interpreting other stuff into his words.

✩₊˚.⋆☾⋆⁺₊✧

As the evening darkened outside, their laughter only grew louder, filling the cozy living room like a second fire. Phainon finally slumped back into the couch, completely drained—not from the day itself, but from losing game after game with no chance of redemption.

“I’m just that good,” Mydei said smugly, arms crossed, his tone a mixture of pride and teasing cruelty.
“Don’t forget who keeps making your coffee,” Phainon muttered with a chuckle, rubbing a hand over his face. His gaze flicked to the clock on the wall—it was already past eight. He stretched and started to push himself up, intent on heading home before it got too late or he annoyed Mydei.
But before he could rise, fingers curled gently around his wrist.

“Ah, right—want something to eat?” Mydei asked abruptly, the words almost tumbling out. His eyes lifted to Phainon’s in a way that felt strangely vulnerable—like a cat pretending not to care while clinging to its favorite person. It was obvious. He didn’t want him to leave.
Phainon blinked, startled by the sudden touch.
His chest tightened for a moment, but then he let out a soft laugh and nodded. “Sure,” he said. “I’m starving anyway.” Eating together… always felt better than eating alone.

“What do you have?” he asked, as Mydei released his wrist.
For a second, Phainon thought he saw something like relief flicker across Mydei’s face. Still, it was quickly buried under his usual calm expression.
“I don’t feel like cooking,” Mydei admitted, rising from the couch. He stretched lazily, then pointed toward the window. “The rain’s stopped. Let’s grab pizza outside.”

Phainon tilted his head toward the glass. Sure enough, the storm had passed, leaving the streets slick with puddles that shimmered under the streetlamps. Children still played in them, shrieking with laughter as they leapt and splashed, completely unbothered by the darkness.
Phainon frowned slightly. “Pizza sounds good… but it’s kind of late. I’m surprised kids are still out playing.”

Mydei stepped closer, his voice low and casual as he reached out to ruffle Phainon’s hair. “Don’t worry—this neighborhood’s safe. Always has been. We look out for each other here.”
The warmth of his hand lingered even after he pulled it away, and Phainon felt something like sunlight stirring in his chest. He ducked his head quickly, hoping Mydei wouldn’t notice the smile tugging at his lips.
“Alright then,” he said softly, brushing at his hair where Mydei had mussed it up. “Pizza it is.”

“Good,” Mydei replied, already tugging on his jacket. “You owe me for losing every single round tonight.”
Phainon rolled his eyes, but his grin betrayed him. “If you’re expecting me to pay, you’re out of luck. Coffee was already charity.”
Mydei glanced back at him, a smirk playing at his lips. “Fine. We’ll share. But I’m picking the toppings.”
Phainon groaned. “God help me.”

“Is it okay if I go out wearing your clothes?” Phainon asked, tugging at the hem of the borrowed shirt. Mydei was already at the door, slipping on his shoes with the kind of energy that made it hard to tell whether he was more excited for pizza or simply for going out with Phainon.

“Of course it is! You look like my bo—” Mydei stopped himself, cheeks flushing as he coughed and waved it off. “—a close friend of mine!”
Phainon raised a brow, amused, and chuckled as he bent down to put on his own shoes. “Right. Close friend. Got it.”

Before Phainon could rise, Mydei spun toward the hallway. “We’ll be back soon, Mimi!” he called, voice loud enough for the whole house to hear. He grabbed two jackets off the rack without breaking stride and tossed one onto Phainon.
“Argh! I don’t need—!” Phainon sputtered, catching the fabric more out of instinct than willingness. He blinked down at it in his arms, his protest dying on his lips. It wasn’t just any jacket—it was simple, black, with a small embroidered blue butterfly near the chest. He noticed how much blue stuff there was in Mydei's house, as if it was waiting for Phainon.

Mydei was already pulling on his own jacket when he noticed Phainon staring. “It’s cold at night,” he said quickly, his tone lighter than the faint pink dusting his cheeks. “Thank me later.”

Phainon slipped it on slowly, the warmth of the fabric wrapping around him in more ways than one. Before he could think of something clever to say, Mydei had already opened the door and grabbed his wrist, tugging him into the cool night air.
Phainon stumbled after him with a laugh. “You really don’t give people a choice, do you?”
“Not when pizza’s on the line,” Mydei shot back, though his grip lingered just a second longer than necessary before letting go.

The air outside was crisp, touched with the damp freshness that only came after rain. Puddles shimmered under the streetlights, and every step sent ripples across their glossy surfaces.
Somewhere nearby, children still laughed as they stomped through the water, their voices carrying down the street like echoes of summer.
Phainon tugged the borrowed jacket a little tighter around himself. It was colder than he expected, but the jacket was soft on the inside, and he couldn’t help but notice the faint scent clinging to it—something clean, faintly herbal, unmistakably Mydei.
He ducked his head, hoping his face wasn’t as red as it felt.

“So,” Mydei said after a moment, hands shoved casually into his pockets, “what’s your pizza order? And don’t say ‘just cheese.’ I’ll judge you.”
Phainon snorted. “What if I like simple things?”
“It won't be,” Mydei shot back, smirking at him. “You’re too dramatic for that.”
Phainon laughed, bumping his shoulder lightly against Mydei’s as they walked side by side down the quiet street. “Bold of you to assume.”
The streetlights painted their shadows long across the pavement, stretching and crossing over each other as if they belonged together.

Mydei tilted his head toward him, his voice softer now.
“Besides… I already know what you’ll pick.”
“Oh?” Phainon arched a brow. “And what’s that?”
Mydei grinned, but didn’t answer, turning his gaze forward again as if the night air had suddenly become very interesting.
Phainon blinked at him, both irritated and weirdly charmed. “You can’t just say that and not tell me.”
“I can. And I will,” Mydei said easily, though his lips curved just enough to betray his amusement.

Phainon sighed dramatically, putting his hands over his mouth. “Unbelievable. I should’ve just gone home.”
“You’d miss me,” Mydei replied without missing a beat.
That shut Phainon up for a moment, his throat going dry as he tried to brush it off with a laugh. “Cocky.”
“Confident,” Mydei corrected, eyes glinting as the glow of the pizzeria’s neon sign came into view at the end of the street.

“It’s closer than I thought,” Phainon said, surprised but secretly pleased. He loved night walks—especially with someone like Mydei—but exhaustion from the day still clung to his shoulders.

Phainon’s lips curved into a small smile after the confession, not one of amusement but of quiet surrender, as though he had finally spoken aloud a thought that had haunted him too long. His eyes softened, their reflection catching the faint light of the stars above, and for a moment, he looked less tired.

“In this life,” he murmured, “I hope you won’t let me go.”
“Of course I won’t, I would never,” Mydei replied, steady and soft, his voice wrapping the quiet night in warmth.
Phainon leaned closer, pressing his lips to Mydei’s. The kiss was slow, deliberate, full of the weight neither had spoken aloud. When they parted, the world felt impossibly still, yet alive with the pulse of their hearts, both beating in unison.
“I hope you can’t hear my heart right now...” Phainon whispered, looking away.
Mydei chuckled softly, a warmth curling around him. “I hear mine more. I worry about you hearing mine.”
"I would love to hear yours." Phainon smiled and put his hand on his heart, hoping that it matched with Mydeis.

“Since this marks our first day,” Mydei said, brushing sand from his hands, “and since I’ve kept you far too long…" Mydei paused again and then continued to talk, "sleep over.”
Phainon raised an eyebrow, knowing he couldn't refuse Mydeis' request, putting on a small act of playfulness.
“Fineeeee—but only if it’s your bed.”

“Obviously,” Mydei grinned, bright and certain.
They lingered, shoulder to shoulder, hands linked, suspended in quiet certainty. Phainon felt it: this closeness—the small and mundane alongside the extraordinary—would not break. Not now, not ever.

"Well, now that this is settled, it's time to go home. Let's go home!" Mydei said, not letting go of Phainon's hand, holding it tighter than before.
Phainon nodded, letting Mydei guide him along the familiar path, the soft crunch of gravel underfoot the only sound that dared to interrupt their silence. The night air was cool against their skin, but their closeness cast its own warmth, a shield against the quiet chill. Every step felt deliberate, slow, as if they were trying to prolong the moment before reality intruded, savoring each second as though the world had shrunk to just the two of them.

The streetlights flickered above, casting pale halos that danced across the pavement. Their shadows stretched long and intertwined, a subtle mirror of the bond that had just solidified between them. Phainon felt the tension in his chest ease with every step, a buoyant lightness he hadn’t known he could carry. The ordinary world, with its dull hums and distant city noises, felt strangely distant, as if it existed somewhere else entirely.

All that mattered was the steady press of Mydei’s hand in his, the rhythm of their shared steps, the quiet pulse of presence that needed no words.
When they reached Phainon’s doorstep, the moment of parting felt impossibly heavy. Mydei lingered, fingers still entwined with his,

They walked past each house, perhaps hoping someone might catch a glimpse of them, to see how love can appear unexpectedly, quietly, yet with a force that turns everything upside down.
How a small nudge, a tiny push out of one’s circle, can rearrange the world in the most astonishingly beautiful ways.
Sometimes, it seemed, happiness didn’t announce itself—it just arrived, and the world, in that fleeting moment, felt magnificent, even if it took time to get there. Seeing someone smile, finding the love you’d always longed for, imagining a future together… these were rare treasures, and tonight, they felt infinite.

As they reached the gate, hands still entwined, it felt as though they were stepping into a life already shared. They stumbled a little in the darkness, trying to see the path ahead while refusing to let go of each other.
“I’ve got your back, Mydei!” Phainon said, laughing, nearly tripping over a stray stone.

“Sure,” Mydei chuckled, “so when I fall, you fall right on top of me.” He fumbled with the front door.
As he almost got it open, he felt how Phainon let go of his hand, when he wanted to ask questions, Phainon hugged him from behind.
“Well… I’ll still be by your side!” Phainon replied, Mydei finally got the door open with a victorious twist.

“I’m sooo tired…” Phainon murmured, resting his head on Mydei’s shoulder.
“Well, you still have to shower. I’m not letting a stinky person into my bed!” Mydei said, gently tugging him further inside, a teasing grin in his voice.
“Soooo mean,” Phainon protested softly.
“That’s how it’ll be… forever,” Mydei replied, laughter in his eyes.
And with that, he closed the door, locking them into a world where they would forever remain unforgettable, unbroken, and inseparable.
